title: For affordable cancer care, go beyond price caps
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to development and management of health; Government policies and interventions · GS3 › Issues relating to intellectual property rights · GS4 › Ethics in business
summary: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP; the editorial argues the cap alone will not make treatment affordable.
ideas: The cap tackles only the middlemen: it limits the margin on sale to patients, not the price at which companies sell to distributors or hospitals. If that starting price is high, the drug stays unaffordable.
GS2 · Health / regulation
Capping trade margins treats the symptom downstream while the real cost is set upstream by the manufacturer's price.
Patents give pricing power: patented cancer drugs face little generic competition, so manufacturers control prices, and earlier caps on the same drugs did not stop prices from rising.
GS3 · IPR and access to medicines
Where patents shut out generics, price caps on margins cannot discipline the manufacturer's price.
Hidden discounts hide the real price: steep discounts on a few units to select corporate hospitals, with most stock sold higher, make the true market price hard for regulators to know.
GS2 · Regulatory capacity
Selective discounts distort the market price, so margin regulation needs scrutiny of manufacturers' prices and transparent sales data.
A blanket cap can backfire: pharmacies have genuine storage and handling costs; a rigid cap could disrupt supplies to underserved areas, and hospitals may pass costs on through higher room rents.
GS2 · Policy design
A blanket price cap risks shortages in underserved areas and cost-shifting by hospitals.
Price control works only with the health system: stronger public health services, wider insurance coverage and more research on generics must accompany the cap.
GS2 · Universal health coverage
Affordable cancer care needs price regulation backed by public health services, insurance and generics.

Trade Margin Rationalisation caps the chain's margin but leaves the manufacturer's price untouched.
Where the cost is set versus where the cap bites
Regulation that targets downstream margins misses upstream pricing power.

Recovering a capped margin through other charges

Balancing affordable medicines with incentives for research
Drug pricing policy must balance access with incentives for innovation.

examples: Ribociclib
A breast cancer drug whose price rose despite margin caps
GS3 · IPR / drug pricing
Ribociclib shows that margin caps fail when patents leave the manufacturer's price unchecked.

GS4
GS2 social justice · GS4 compassion
When cancer drugs are unaffordable, patients delay treatment or skip doses, turning cost into lost lives.

Limits of the public health system and the private sector's role: affordable medicines are part of universal coverage.
Section 3(d) and the Novartis case: patents versus access to affordable medicines.

trend.t: Health questions moved from goals and access (MDGs 2013, universal coverage 2015, community-level care 2018) to the State's moral and practical role (primary health 2021) and, most recently, to containing the marketisation of healthcare (2024). In GS3, patents and access to medicines appeared in 2013.
trend.watch: The balance between the State and the private sector in health has come in 2015 and 2024. Regulation of the health market is a must-study area.
focus: State regulation of drug prices and hospital charges

answer.t: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP, where intermediaries added an average 170% mark-up (NPPA).

pts.t: Margin caps do not cover the manufacturer's price to distributors and hospitals.
pts.ex: Ribociclib's cost rose from ₹58,000 to ₹78,000 despite 2019 caps.

pts.t: Patented drugs face little generic competition, so prices stay high.
Selective discounts to corporate hospitals hide the real market price.
Hospitals may recover capped margins through room rents and other charges.
Rigid caps may make supply to underserved areas unviable for pharmacies.
Low insurance coverage leaves patients paying out of pocket.
pts.ex: Patients delay treatment or skip doses.

pts.t: Mandatory reporting of sales and discounts.
More research on and production of generic versions.
Strengthen public hospitals and coverage for cancer care.
Allow for legitimate storage and handling costs.

answer.t: Price caps can lower bills, but only a strong public health system can make cancer care truly affordable.

title: May make banks pay digital arrest victims if no due diligence: SC
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Ananthakrishnan G)
syllabus: GS3 › Challenges to internal security through communication networks; Basics of cyber security; Money laundering · GS2 › Structure and functioning of the judiciary; Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies · GS4 › Compassion towards the weaker sections; Probity
summary: In its own case on digital arrest scams, the Supreme Court said it may make banks compensate victims and face prosecution where poor due diligence enabled the fraud, and faulted the RBI for 'soft pedalling'.
ideas: A fraud on the economy: the Court called digital arrest the biggest financial fraud on the country's economy, running into thousands of crores; it is now a systemic threat, not a scattered crime.
GS3 · Cybercrime / financial security
Digital arrest scams, called by the Supreme Court the biggest financial fraud on the economy, have become a systemic cyber-security threat.

Accountability shifted to banks: the Court proposes that banks compensate victims and face prosecution if lapses enabled the fraud, with a mandatory rule to suspend unusual transactions until full verification.
GS3 banking · GS2 judiciary
Placing liability on banks that fail due diligence puts the cost of fraud on the institution best placed to stop it.
A regulator too soft: the Court faulted the RBI for consulting banks while the Court sought action against them, and called 'guidelines' too weak a word; rules need teeth.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies
Advisory guidelines invite regulatory soft-pedalling; mandatory rules with liability make regulators effective.
Insiders in the fraud: the Court noted that some bank officials are involved; the Attorney General said not every employee colludes and some have acted to stop frauds.
GS3 · Insider threat in banking
Insider collusion turns banks from the first line of defence into a channel for cyber fraud.

A three-level response: the Attorney General said prevention works through awareness, bank checks at the right stage, and RBI and MeitY rules due by December, and that complaints have fallen since the Court stepped in.
GS3 · Way forward
Countering digital arrest needs awareness, bank-level checks and binding regulation working together.
keywords: Scammers posing as officials hold victims in a fake 'arrest' over video calls until they pay
Digital arrest scams exploit fear of authority rather than technical loopholes.
Manipulating people psychologically rather than hacking systems
Digital arrest is social engineering: the weakest link is human fear, not software.
Making the party that can most easily prevent a loss bear it
Liability should rest with the actor best placed to stop fraud: the bank.
A regulator going easy on those it regulates
The Court's rebuke of the RBI warns against regulatory soft-pedalling.
Insider collusion makes internal controls as important as cyber defences.
A court acting on its own, without a petition
Through suo motu action, the Court made a scattered crime a matter of national accountability.
examples: The Supreme Court's suo motu case
The Court took up digital arrest scams on its own, without waiting for a petition
GS2 · Judiciary / people-centric governance
The Supreme Court's suo motu case on digital arrests shows the judiciary stepping in to protect citizens where others were slow.
Victim's money stays untouched, the bank pays
The proposed rule puts the burden on the strong institution, not the frightened individual
GS4
GS4 · Compassion towards the weaker sections
Making banks, not frightened victims, bear the loss reflects compassion towards the vulnerable.
Bank officials helping fraudsters
The Court noted some bank officials are involved in digital arrest frauds
GS4
GS4 · Corruption and probity
Insider collusion by bank officials is corruption that betrays the public trust placed in institutions.
Mandatory checks, not soft guidelines
The Court pushed the RBI to make transaction checks compulsory rather than advisory
GS2 · Proactive governance in regulation
Regulators must act before harm spreads: binding rules, not advisory guidelines.
pyqs: Types of cybercrime and measures: digital arrest is the newest major type, with bank liability as a measure.
A comprehensive cyber security strategy: financial fraud shows gaps across banks, regulators and citizens.
The growth of PIL and a powerful Supreme Court: suo motu action on digital arrest is a fresh example.
Independent, effective regulators: the Court's rebuke of the RBI's soft-pedalling.

trend.t: Cyber questions have come almost every year: cyber warfare (2013), the cyber security policy (2015), threats and frameworks (2017), data security (2018), CyberDome (2019), types of cybercrime (2020), cross-border attacks (2021) and a national strategy (2022). The focus has moved from threats to the state towards crimes against citizens and the institutional response.
trend.watch: Cyber security appeared every year from 2017 to 2022. It is a must-study GS3 area, now with financial fraud at its centre.
focus: Types of cybercrime, especially financial fraud
Institutional liability of banks and regulators
National cyber security strategy and coordination

potential: "Digital arrest scams expose gaps in both banking safeguards and regulatory enforcement." Discuss, and suggest a framework to protect citizens. (15 marks)
Should banks be held liable for losses suffered by victims of cyber fraud? Critically examine. (10 marks)
Examine the role of the Supreme Court's suo motu interventions in addressing gaps in governance, with recent examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: Should banks be held liable for losses suffered by victims of cyber fraud? Critically examine.
parts: Introduction: the Supreme Court's proposal in one line

answer.t: In October 2026 the Supreme Court proposed making banks compensate digital arrest victims where failure of due diligence enabled the fraud.

pts.t: Banks see transactions in real time and can stop unusual transfers.
Some frauds involve bank officials; liability strengthens internal controls.
Victims act under fear and manipulation; the system must protect them.
Liability pushes banks to invest in fraud detection.
Customers may become careless if banks always pay.
Compensation costs may be passed on to all customers.
Excessive holds may delay legitimate transactions.
Link liability to proven lapses in due diligence.
Mandatory RBI rules rather than advisory guidelines.
Citizen awareness that no agency 'arrests' anyone over a video call.

answer.t: Liability tied to due diligence can make banks the first line of defence against cyber fraud rather than its conduit.

title: Inter-State Council is a meeting point that has withered away. It must be rebuilt
syllabus: GS2 › Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; Issues and challenges pertaining to the federal structure; Centre-State relations; Constitutional bodies
summary: Shashi Tharoor argues that decisions like delimitation need the states' voice, and the Inter-State Council under Article 263, dormant for years, must be revived as an autonomous forum for Centre-state consultation.
evolution: Article 263 empowers the President to set up a council for Centre-state coordination.
Sarkaria Commission calls the dormant Inter-State Council the 'missing link'; the Council is constituted in 1990.
Long gaps between meetings; the Council works as an appendage of the Home Ministry.
Debate over a delimitation bill; Tharoor calls for reviving the Council before such decisions.
ideas: States must be heard on delimitation: deciding it in Parliament alone bypasses the states, an essential part of the federal system.
GS2 · Federalism / delimitation
A change as basic as delimitation should follow a national conversation that includes the states, not Parliament alone.
Article 263 envisioned a meeting point: the founders created the Inter-State Council to balance a strongly centralised Constitution in a diverse country.
GS2 · Constitutional bodies
Article 263 was meant to temper India's centralising Constitution with a forum for Centre-state coordination.
The 'missing link': the Council lay dormant for four decades and was set up only in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice.
GS2 · Centre-state relations
The Sarkaria Commission called the dormant Inter-State Council the missing link in India's federal equilibrium.
Withered by design: without operational autonomy or regular meetings, it became an appendage of the Home Ministry, preferring unilateral policymaking over dialogue.
GS2 · Institutional weakness
Without operational autonomy or regular meetings, the Inter-State Council has become a minor arm of the Home Ministry.
Its atrophy erodes trust, especially with opposition-ruled states, as policy on tax, health, environment and security cuts across jurisdictions.
GS2 · Cooperative vs confrontational federalism
When the Inter-State Council is dormant, top-down policy breeds friction, especially with opposition-ruled states.
Rebuild it: an independent statutory secretariat, fixed meetings of the PM and CMs, and a role in major reforms, scheme reviews and inter-state disputes, giving 'cooperative federalism' a platform.
GS2 · Way forward
A revived Inter-State Council would give 'cooperative federalism' a platform, not just a slogan.

Article 263 empowers the President to set up an Inter-State Council for Centre-state coordination.

Centre and states working together as partners
Cooperative federalism has remained 'a platitude without a platform'.
Gradual weakening of an institution through neglect
Institutional atrophy has left a void at the heart of Indian federalism.
Redrawing seats and their distribution among states
Delimitation without the states' voice risks a federal crisis.
Mutual suspicion between the Centre and states
The Council's atrophy has deepened the Centre-state trust deficit.
examples: Inter-State Council (1990)

pyqs: Directly usable: drawbacks of cooperative federalism; a dormant Inter-State Council is one.
Cooperation, competition, confrontation: a dormant Council tilts the balance to confrontation.
Recent changes in Centre-state relations; measures to build trust include reviving the Inter-State Council.
Dispute-resolution mechanisms in the federal framework: the Inter-State Council is the constitutional one.
Regional parties seek autonomy; a forum for states' views eases the tension.
Federalism as a basic feature is weakened when states are not consulted.

trend.t: Federalism has been asked almost every year: cooperative federalism (2015), cooperation versus confrontation (2020), national versus regional parties (2022), recent changes in Centre-state relations (2024), fiscal relations (2025) and dispute-resolution mechanisms (2026), alongside the Governor (2022, 2026) and Article 356 (2023). The focus has moved from the nature of Indian federalism to the institutions that should make it work.
trend.watch: Centre-state relations come up in nearly every GS2 paper. Institutional mechanisms (Inter-State Council, Zonal Councils, GST Council, Finance Commission) and delimitation are must-study.
focus: Reviving the Inter-State Council and other Centre-state forums

practice.q: The Inter-State Council has remained a 'missing link' in India's federal structure. Examine the reasons for its ineffectiveness and suggest measures to make it a genuine platform for cooperative federalism.

answer.t: Envisaged under Article 263 and set up only in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice, the Inter-State Council has met rarely, leaving Centre-state dialogue without a forum.

pts.t: A forum where states shape national policy in a diverse country.
Tax, health, environment and security cut across jurisdictions.
Delimitation and resource sharing need states' consent.
A neutral platform for Centre-state and inter-state disputes.
Regular dialogue reduces friction and litigation.
States can assess the local impact of central schemes.
It works as an appendage of the Home Ministry.
Years pass between meetings despite the obligation to meet.
Its recommendations do not bind the Centre.
Governments favour central decisions or informal deals.
Opposition-ruled states see it as a Centre-controlled forum.
NITI Aayog and other bodies dilute its role.
Convene the PM, key ministers and CMs at regular intervals.
A statutory secretariat with civil servants and experts.
Require consultation on delimitation, major reforms and state-specific laws.
Use it for inter-state disputes on water, resources and infrastructure.
A working model of shared decision-making.
No new law is needed; Article 263 already allows it.

answer.t: Reviving the Inter-State Council would give cooperative federalism a platform, turning Centre-state relations from confrontation into partnership.
